subject: biology
title: Pathogens and disease
summary: The main types of pathogens (bacteria, viruses, fungi, protozoa and parasites), how infectious diseases spread, how they differ from non-infectious diseases, and how hygiene reduces spread.
body:
A **disease** is any condition that stops part of the body from working normally. Some diseases are caused by tiny living things (or particles) that invade the body, while others come from our genes, our lifestyle or our environment. Knowing what causes a disease and how it spreads is the first step in preventing it, which is why handwashing, clean water and safe food handling matter so much in everyday life.

## Think of it like this

### A virus is like malware that hijacks your phone

Malware can't do anything sitting by itself; it has to get onto a phone and use that phone's processor to run and make copies of itself, which it then sends out to other phones. A **virus** works the same way. It's just genetic material (DNA or RNA) in a protein coat, and it can't grow or reproduce on its own. It enters a **host** cell, takes over the cell's machinery to make copies of itself, and the new viruses often burst out, destroying the cell. **Bacteria**, by contrast, are like a whole separate device: complete cells with their own machinery that can reproduce by themselves.

*Where the analogy breaks down:* malware is written by people on purpose, while viruses are natural and have no goal; they just copy themselves when they get the chance. Also, phones can be wiped and restored, but cells destroyed by a virus are gone and have to be replaced by the body.

### Transmission is like a rumour spreading around school

A rumour spreads from person to person: whispered face to face (**direct contact**), written on a note left on a desk for someone else to pick up (**indirect contact** via a **fomite**), shouted across the canteen so everyone nearby hears it (**droplets and airborne spread**), or carried by someone who passes it on without believing it themselves. That last one is like a **vector**: a mosquito carries the malaria **pathogen** from one host to another without getting the disease. **Hygiene** is like refusing to pass the rumour on: breaking the chain of **transmission** at any link stops the spread.

*Where the analogy breaks down:* a rumour can be passed on by anyone who hears it, but a pathogen only causes disease if it gets into a suitable host and survives the body's defences. Also, many people catch a pathogen without showing symptoms, while a rumour you've heard is obvious.

### A vector is like a food delivery driver

A delivery rider picks up an order from one place and drops it at another, but doesn't eat it themselves. A **vector** is the same: the mosquito picks up the malaria-causing **protozoan** from one person's blood and drops it into the next person when it bites, without getting malaria. Removing standing water where mosquitoes breed is like closing the road the drivers use.

*Where the analogy breaks down:* a delivery driver just carries a sealed bag, but in many vectors the pathogen actually lives and develops inside the vector's body before it can be passed on.

### In real life

Washing your hands with soap for at least the time it takes to sing a short song is effective because soap lifts pathogens off the skin and breaks apart the outer layer of some viruses. Food safety rules in the school canteen, such as cooking chicken thoroughly and keeping food cold, are there to stop bacteria like *Salmonella* causing food poisoning.

## Key ideas

### Infectious and non-infectious disease

An **infectious disease** is caused by a **pathogen**, which is an organism or agent that causes disease. Infectious diseases can pass from one host to another. Examples include the common cold, influenza, tuberculosis and malaria. The organism that a pathogen lives in is called the **host**.

A **non-infectious disease** is not caused by a pathogen and cannot be caught from another person. Causes include:

- **Genetic** factors, such as cystic fibrosis, which is inherited from parents.
- **Lifestyle** factors, such as smoking, poor diet or lack of exercise, which raise the risk of heart disease, type 2 diabetes and some cancers.
- **Environmental** factors, such as too much ultraviolet (UV) radiation from the sun, which can lead to skin cancer.
- **Nutritional deficiencies**, such as scurvy from too little vitamin C.

Many conditions have more than one cause. For example, a person's genes can make heart disease more likely, and a poor diet then adds to that risk.

### Types of pathogens

| Pathogen | Cellular? | Size and features | Example diseases |
|---|---|---|---|
| Bacteria | Yes, prokaryotic (no nucleus) | Single cells with a cell wall and circular DNA | Tuberculosis, strep throat, food poisoning (*Salmonella*) |
| Viruses | No | Much smaller than bacteria; genetic material inside a protein coat | Influenza, measles, COVID-19, common cold |
| Fungi | Yes, eukaryotic | Single cells (yeasts) or thread-like hyphae | Tinea (athlete's foot), thrush |
| Protozoa | Yes, eukaryotic | Single cells, often able to move | Malaria (*Plasmodium*), giardiasis |
| Parasites (worms and insects) | Yes, multicellular | Live on or in a host and feed from it | Tapeworm, head lice, scabies mites |

**Bacteria** are single-celled **prokaryotes**, meaning their cells have no nucleus. Many bacteria are harmless or even helpful (for example, those in your gut that help with digestion). Disease-causing bacteria harm us by damaging cells and by releasing **toxins**, which are poisonous chemicals.

**Viruses** are not made of cells. A virus is a small package of genetic material (DNA or RNA) inside a protein coat. Viruses cannot grow or reproduce on their own. They must enter a host cell and take over its machinery to make copies of themselves. The new viruses often burst out of the cell, destroying it. Because they are **non-cellular**, viruses are not usually described as living in the same way bacteria are.

**Fungi** are eukaryotes, meaning their cells have a nucleus. Most fungal infections in healthy people affect the skin, nails or moist areas of the body.

**Protozoa** are single-celled eukaryotes. The protozoan that causes malaria is carried by mosquitoes and infects red blood cells.

**Parasites** in the wider sense include multicellular animals that live on (**ectoparasites**, such as lice) or in (**endoparasites**, such as tapeworms) a host, taking nutrients and harming it. Strictly, all pathogens live off a host, but in school biology "parasite" usually means these larger organisms.

### How infectious diseases spread

The process of a pathogen passing from one host to another is called **transmission**. The main routes are:

- **Direct contact**: touching an infected person, such as through skin contact or kissing (for example, cold sores).
- **Indirect contact**: touching a contaminated object, called a **fomite**, such as a door handle or phone, then touching your mouth, nose or eyes.
- **Droplets and airborne spread**: coughing and sneezing release tiny drops carrying pathogens, such as influenza viruses.
- **Contaminated food and water**: eating undercooked food or drinking unclean water, such as *Salmonella* food poisoning or cholera.
- **Vectors**: a **vector** is an organism that carries a pathogen from one host to another without itself getting the disease. Mosquitoes carrying malaria are the classic example.
- **Body fluids**: blood and other fluids, such as through shared needles (for example, hepatitis B).

### Hygiene and prevention

Breaking the chain of transmission stops a disease spreading. Good **hygiene** means practices that keep us and our surroundings clean to reduce pathogens:

- Washing hands with soap removes pathogens from the skin and breaks apart the outer layer of some viruses.
- Covering coughs and sneezes, and staying home when sick, reduces droplet spread.
- Cooking food thoroughly and storing it cold slows or kills bacteria.
- Treating drinking water and having proper sewage systems stops waterborne disease.
- Removing standing water and using insect repellent reduces mosquito vectors.
- **Sterilising** medical equipment kills all microorganisms on it.

## Worked examples

### Example 1: Identifying a pathogen

**Scenario:** A pathogen is examined with a microscope. It has no nucleus, has a cell wall, and can be grown on a nutrient plate in the lab. What type of pathogen is it?

**Step 1:** It has cells, so it is not a virus.
**Step 2:** It has no nucleus, so it is a prokaryote. Fungi and protozoa have a nucleus.
**Step 3:** It grows on its own on a nutrient plate. Viruses could not do this because they need host cells.

**Answer:** It is a bacterium.

### Example 2: Choosing the right prevention

**Scenario:** In a town, many people develop diarrhoea after a flood. Most of them live in the same area and use the same water supply. Suggest the likely route of transmission and one way to control it.

**Step 1:** Look for what the sick people share. They share a water supply, and floods can wash sewage into water.
**Step 2:** The likely route is contaminated water.
**Step 3:** Control means breaking that route: boil drinking water or supply treated bottled water, and repair sewage systems.

**Answer:** Waterborne transmission. Boiling or treating drinking water would reduce the spread.

## Common mistakes

- Thinking all bacteria are harmful. Most are harmless, and many are useful.
- Calling viruses cells or saying they can reproduce on their own. They need a host cell.
- Saying a vector "has" the disease. A vector carries the pathogen, usually without becoming ill.
- Assuming non-infectious diseases are always caused by lifestyle. Genetic and environmental causes count too.
- Mixing up "infectious" (caused by a pathogen) with "contagious" in every case. Some infectious diseases, such as malaria, do not spread directly from person to person; they need a vector.

## Exam tips

- Be ready to classify a disease as infectious or non-infectious and give a reason based on its cause.
- When describing a pathogen, name its type and a key feature (for example, "a virus, which is non-cellular and needs a host cell to reproduce").
- For prevention questions, link the method directly to the transmission route it breaks. This is what earns the mark.

## Tips to remember

- **Five pathogen types, a made-up trick: "Bad Viruses Find People Pleasant"** – Bacteria, Viruses, Fungi, Protozoa, Parasites.
- **A virus is a hijacker.** It's not a cell and can't reproduce on its own, so it takes over a host cell's machinery to copy itself.
- **A vector is a delivery driver, not the customer.** A mosquito carries the malaria pathogen but usually doesn't get sick itself.
- **Infectious = can be caught (caused by a pathogen). Non-infectious = can't be caught** (genetic, lifestyle, environmental or nutritional causes).
- **Most bacteria are friends.** Only some cause disease, and many (like gut bacteria) are helpful.
- **Break the chain:** handwashing, covering coughs, cooking food properly, clean water and getting rid of mosquito breeding sites all stop transmission.

## Key terms

- **Disease** — a condition that stops part of the body working normally.
- **Pathogen** — an organism or agent that causes disease.
- **Host** — the organism a pathogen lives in or on.
- **Infectious disease** — a disease caused by a pathogen that can pass between hosts.
- **Non-infectious disease** — a disease not caused by a pathogen; it cannot be caught.
- **Prokaryote** — a cell without a nucleus, such as a bacterium.
- **Toxin** — a poisonous chemical released by some pathogens.
- **Transmission** — the passing of a pathogen from one host to another.
- **Fomite** — an object that carries pathogens between people.
- **Vector** — an organism that carries a pathogen between hosts.
- **Hygiene** — practices that keep people and surroundings clean to reduce disease.

## Summary

- Pathogens include bacteria, viruses, fungi, protozoa and parasites.
- Viruses are non-cellular and can only reproduce inside host cells; the others are cellular.
- Infectious diseases are caused by pathogens; non-infectious diseases come from genes, lifestyle, environment or diet.
- Pathogens spread by contact, fomites, droplets, food and water, vectors and body fluids.
- Hygiene and other prevention methods work by breaking the chain of transmission.

questions.prompt: Which of the following pathogens is non-cellular?
questions.explanation: Viruses are made of genetic material inside a protein coat and are not cells. Bacteria are a tempting choice because they are very small, but they are complete single cells (prokaryotes).

options.B: An object, such as a door handle, that carries pathogens
options.C: An organism that carries a pathogen from one host to another
options.D: A person who is immune to a disease

questions.explanation: A vector is a living organism, such as a mosquito, that carries a pathogen between hosts. Option B describes a fomite, which is non-living.

questions.prompt: Why can't viruses be grown on a nutrient plate in the way bacteria can?

options.A: Viruses are too large to fit on the plate
options.B: Viruses only reproduce inside living host cells
options.C: Viruses are killed by the nutrients

questions.explanation: Viruses have no cell machinery of their own and must take over a host cell to make copies. Saying the nutrients kill them is wrong; nutrients simply cannot help a virus reproduce.

Cystic fibrosis is a genetic condition inherited from parents, not caused by a pathogen. Malaria might seem non-infectious because it does not spread directly between people, but it is caused by a protozoan pathogen carried by mosquitoes.

questions.prompt: Washing hands with soap mainly helps prevent disease by:

options.D: removing pathogens before they can enter the body

questions.explanation: Soap and water remove pathogens from the hands, breaking contact and fomite transmission. Handwashing does not make antibodies; antibodies are made by white blood cells.

questions.prompt: A pathogen has a nucleus, is a single cell and can move. It infects red blood cells after a mosquito bite. What type of pathogen is it most likely to be?
questions.explanation: A single-celled eukaryote that can move is a protozoan, like the one that causes malaria. A bacterium is single-celled but has no nucleus, so it does not fit.

questions.prompt: Several students fall ill after eating chicken at a barbecue where the meat was pink in the middle. Which control method best targets the cause?

options.D: Cooking meat all the way through

questions.explanation: Undercooked meat can carry bacteria such as Salmonella, and thorough cooking kills them. Covering coughs targets droplet spread, which is not the route here.

questions.prompt: A student says, "Heart disease is non-infectious, so it must be caused only by lifestyle." Which response is best?

options.A: Correct, because only lifestyle causes non-infectious disease
options.B: Incorrect, because heart disease is caused by bacteria
options.C: Incorrect, because genetic factors can also contribute
options.D: Correct, because genes only cause infectious diseases

questions.explanation: Non-infectious diseases can have genetic, lifestyle and environmental causes, often together. Option B is wrong because heart disease is not caused by a pathogen.
